_about: Rule corpus for the Prosody Engine Lab. Source: F. W. Pritchett & K. A. Khaliq, Urdu Meter: A Practical Handbook (sections cited per rule). kind: strict = never violated; flexible = allowed variation with a likelihood; transcription = Urdu-script under-specification (a hypothesis about what the text means, not a prosodic licence). likelihood.prior values come from the handbook's own wording via the scale in _likelihood_scale; the `evidence` block on each rule is written by learn.js from the Ghalib+Mir corpora and is never edited by hand.

rules.title: What counts as a letter

condition.letters: alif..ye, tashdiid duplicate, madd over alif, medial hamzah

rules.effect: only these are counted when dividing into syllables
rules.learner: Only letters count: every letter of the alphabet, the doubled letter of a tashdīd, alif madd, and a hamza inside a word.

rules.title: zer, zabar, pesh are not letters
rules.effect: ignored when counting letters
rules.learner: Short-vowel marks are not letters, so they never make a syllable longer.

rules.title: do-chashmī he of aspiration is not a letter

condition.ascii: h directly after one of these consonants

rules.effect: metrically invisible
rules.learner: The ھ of bh, ph, th, kh… is part of the consonant, not a letter: bhii is one two-letter syllable.

rules.title: nūn-e ghunnah is not a letter
rules.effect: metrically invisible
rules.learner: The nasal ں (;N) colours the vowel but is not a letter: me;N is two letters, one syllable.

rules.title: tashdīd writes a second letter
rules.effect: the letter counts twice
rules.learner: A tashdīd doubles its letter: mu;habbat is mu-;hab-bat (- = =).

rules.title: the dotless ye under hamza is not a letter
rules.effect: only the hamza counts
rules.learner: In ئ only the hamza counts; the little ye it sits on is just a seat.

rules.title: ((ain and medial hamza behave as consonants
rules.effect: treated as consonants even when not pronounced
rules.learner: ع and a medial ء are consonants for scansion, even where you barely hear them.

rules.title: h'h counts as one h
rules.effect: only one h is scanned: kah'h (=), naalah'haa = naa-la-haa (= - =)
rules.learner: In Pritchett's romanisation an apostrophe between two h's (kah'h, naalah'haa) means they are scanned as one.

rules.title: A syllable has one or two letters
rules.effect: every syllable is 1 or 2 letters (4.2 and 4.3 conjuncts are the named exceptions)
rules.learner: Every syllable is one letter or two, never more.

rules.title: Start with a consonant wherever possible
rules.effect: syllables are C+C, C+V or C alone; a, aa, a+V, a+C only at the start of a word
rules.learner: Syllables begin with a consonant; only the first syllable of a word may begin with a vowel.

rules.title: Hamza is never the second letter of a syllable
rules.effect: forbidden
rules.learner: A hamza always starts a syllable; it can never close one.

rules.title: Alif madd is a syllable by itself
rules.effect: always one long syllable, and signals a new syllable
rules.learner: آ is always its own long syllable: aadmii is aa-d-mii (= - =).

rules.title: Final ii after ((ain / hamza as consonant y
rules.effect: the ii may be the consonant y: sa((ii = sa((-y (= -)

consonant.handbook: the amphibious role of o ii e as vowels or consonants (7)

rules.learner: The ی of سعی can be a consonant: sa((-y, not sa-((ii.

rules.title: Divide by normal prose pronunciation

condition.ascii: short vowels written in the transcription fix the breaks

rules.effect: a consonant followed by a vowel starts a syllable; a vowelless consonant closes the syllable before it
rules.learner: Break the word where you hear the breaks: ka-bhii, mul-k, qis-m.

rules.title: Three-letter three-consonant words
rules.effect: most split CC-C (qis-m, mul-k); a minority C-CC (va-raq, ;Ga-zal)
rules.learner: Three consonants and no written vowel: usually two-then-one (qis-m), sometimes one-then-two (;Ga-zal).

rules.title: Two letters long, one letter short
rules.effect: 2-letter syllable = long (=), 1-letter = short (-); a flexible (x) syllable is a 2-letter one that may be used short
rules.learner: Two letters make a long syllable, one letter a short one. A one-letter syllable can never be made long.

rules.title: The common flexible monosyllables
rules.effect: x: long or short as the meter needs

likelihood.handbook: flexible (particles, pronouns, postpositions: almost always)

rules.learner: kaa, ke, kii, se, ne, hai, to, jo… are flexible: they can take a long or a short beat.

rules.title: Other C+V / C+h monosyllables
rules.effect: normally long; treat as potentially flexible when finding the meter

likelihood.handbook: not on the list: not flexible, but can be taken as long; ii/e/h more likely flexible than o, than aa

rules.learner: A one-syllable word not on the flexible list is normally long.

rules.title: taa, go, yaa are virtually always long
rules.effect: long

likelihood.handbook: virtually ALWAYS LONG

rules.learner: taa, go and yaa are always long.

rules.title: Arabic and Persian noun monosyllables are long
rules.effect: long

likelihood.handbook: almost always long, with no flexibility possible

rules.learner: Persian and Arabic nouns such as mai, jaa, ruu are always long.

rules.title: Vocative ai
rules.effect: long (archaic: sometimes short)

likelihood.handbook: nowadays always long; in archaic usage sometimes short

rules.learner: The vocative ai ('O…') is long.

rules.title: vaa;N and yaa;N
rules.effect: long; in older poetry once in a while short

likelihood.handbook: always long nowadays, but once in a while may, in older poetry, occur as short

rules.learner: vaa;N and yaa;N are long (older poets occasionally shorten them).

rules.title: kyaa, kyuu;N, jyuu;N: one long syllable
rules.effect: one long syllable despite the cluster; almost never flexible

likelihood.handbook: always scanned long; almost never used as flexible

rules.learner: kyaa, kyuu;N and jyuu;N are single long syllables.

rules.title: bah, kih, nah are short
rules.effect: short (Mir: sometimes long)

likelihood.handbook: ALWAYS SHORT in modern usage; Mir treats kih and nah as long from time to time

rules.learner: bah, kih and nah are short. (Mir sometimes lengthens kih and nah.)

rules.title: aur: (= -) or (=)
rules.effect: au-r (= -) or one long (=)
rules.learner: aur can be two syllables (au-r, = -) or one long (=). It is the commonest source of scanning mistakes.

rules.title: aur as one syllable: its weight
rules.effect: the handbook gives (=); Ghalib also uses it short (tuu aur aaraa))ish-e, meter #14)

likelihood.handbook: or simply as one long syllable (=)

rules.learner: Read as one syllable, aur is normally long; a few lines of Ghalib need it short.

rules.title: Repeated monosyllable
rules.effect: first long, second may be flexible (Mir's kyaa kyaa (= -))

likelihood.handbook: this is rare

rules.learner: In a repeated word like kyaa kyaa, the second may be shortened; this is rare.

rules.title: Word-final ii / e / h syllables are flexible
rules.effect: x

likelihood.handbook: almost always flexible

rules.learner: A word-final -ii, -e or -ah (dil kii, siinah) can be long or short.

rules.title: Word-final o / aa syllables are often flexible
rules.effect: x; Indic (esp. verbs) more than Persian/Arabic; o more than aa

likelihood.handbook: often treated as flexible; in some words always long

rules.learner: A word-final -aa or -o is often flexible in Indic words (rahaa, - x) but stays long in many Persian/Arabic ones (rihaa, - =).

rules.title: Medial flexibility: ko))ii, aa))iinah
rules.effect: ko))ii (x x), aa))iinah (= x x)

likelihood.handbook: only a VERY few exceptions

rules.learner: Flexible syllables are almost always word-final; ko))ii and aa))iinah are the famous exceptions.

rules.title: Future verb forms
rules.effect: jaa))egaa (= x x)

likelihood.handbook: equally flexible

rules.learner: In jaa))egaa the middle syllable is flexible too (= x x).

rules.title: -uu / -o before a final hamza ending

condition.pattern: C+uu or C+o immediately before a final hamza+vowel syllable (plural -))o;N/-))e;N, -))ii, -))e)

rules.effect: aa;Nsuu))o;N (= x x), juu))e;N (x x); glossary duu))ii (x x), muu))e (- x)

likelihood.handbook: flexibility sometimes remains ... chiefly with words ending in uu

rules.learner: Before a plural ending, a -uu can stay flexible: aa;Nsuu))o;N (= x x).

rules.title: Alternate syllable divisions
rules.effect: barhaman (= - =) or (- = =); :tar;h (= -) or (- =); Arabic CCC-initial barkat (= =) or (- - =)

alt.handbook: at the poet's pleasure / original Arabic

rules.learner: A few consonant-heavy words may be divided two ways: :tar-;h or :ta-ra;h.

rules.title: Flexible spellings are scanned as written
rules.effect: the spelling tells you the scansion
rules.learner: meraa (= x) and miraa (- x) are both correct; the spelling shows which the poet wants.

rules.title: Final n and ;N interchange
rules.effect: bayaan (- = -) vs bayaa;N (- =); gulistaa;N vs gulistaan

swapped.handbook: 7: n / ;N confusion is a possible copying error

rules.learner: Changing a final n to ;N removes a short syllable (bayaan → bayaa;N).

rules.title: Optional tashdīd in perfect forms

condition.key: very-often (rakh-, chakh-) | sometimes (pak-, u;Th-) | rarely (likh-) | noun (dukaan, shakar)

rules.effect: rakhaa (- x) or rakkhaa (= x)

likelihood.handbook: very often / sometimes / rarely; nouns: more often absent

rules.learner: rakhaa is often read rak-khaa with an unwritten tashdīd; likhaa rarely is.

rules.title: Word-grafting
rules.effect: read the pair as one word, dropping the alif (aa;xir is → aa;xiris, = - =)

graft.handbook: certainly occurs less than half the time

rules.learner: When a word ends in a consonant and the next starts with a / aa, you may run them together: aap agar → aa-pa-gar.

rules.title: Grafting after a final gol he

condition.first_ends: h after a short vowel (kih, siinah)

rules.effect: as 3.1; the handbook does not single this case out, so it is measured separately
rules.learner: A word ending in a written h (kih, siinah) can graft like any consonant-final word, but it is uncommon.

rules.title: Grafting through a final ii / e / o
rules.effect: the vowel is read as a consonant (y / v) to allow grafting
rules.learner: Very rarely a final ii / e / o turns into y / v so the next word can graft onto it.

rules.title: Grafting onto ((ain
rules.effect: (( treated as alif (Mir: ;xaak ((anbar → ;xaa-k((an-bar)

graft.handbook: such liberties are no longer taken

rules.learner: Mir once grafted onto a word starting with ع; later poets never do.

rules.title: iẓāfat on a consonant

condition.last_letter: consonant (incl. gol he after a short vowel)

rules.effect: the iẓāfat joins the last letter as one flexible syllable: lab-e = la-be (- x), mulk-e = mul-ke (= x)

likelihood.handbook: apart from two-consonant Arabic words, never broken

rules.learner: An iẓāfat after a consonant borrows that consonant: dil-e = di-le. The rest of the word does not change.

rules.title: Arabic C+C monosyllable + iẓāfat: optional tashdīd

condition.word: two consonant letters with a short vowel between (fan, ;xa:t)

rules.effect: fa-ne (- x) or fan-ne (= x)

tashdid.handbook: optional, or with some words compulsory

rules.learner: Short Arabic words like fan or ;xa:t may double their last letter before an iẓāfat: fan-ne.

rules.title: iẓāfat on alif
rules.effect: final aa is always long; the iẓāfat (written e / ئے / hamza / zer) is its own flexible syllable: vafaa-e (- = x)
rules.learner: After -aa, the iẓāfat is its own syllable and the -aa can no longer be shortened.

rules.title: iẓāfat on vowel o / uu / au
rules.effect: usually like alif (kuu-e, = x); with au usually the vao becomes a consonant (jau-e = ja-ve, - x)

likelihood.handbook: usually treated like alif; in some cases (usually au) the o becomes a consonant

rules.learner: After -uu the iẓāfat stands alone (kuu-e); after -au the vao turns into v (ja-ve).

rules.title: iẓāfat on ii
rules.effect: as a rule ii becomes consonant y: sho;xii-e = sho-;xi-ye (= - x); rarely a separate (short) iẓāfat after a long ii
rules.learner: -ii + iẓāfat normally becomes -i-ye: sho;xii-e = sho-;xi-ye.

rules.title: iẓāfat on e / ai
rules.effect: e becomes consonant y: mai-e = ma-ye (- x)
rules.learner: -e / -ai + iẓāfat becomes -a-ye: mai-e = ma-ye.

rules.title: Weight of the iẓāfat syllable

condition.key: joined (on a consonant) | after-aa | after-o | after-ii (separate)

rules.effect: x; the separate iẓāfat after a long vowel is most often short

likelihood.handbook: one flexible syllable; after o most often short; after a long ii almost always short

rules.learner: The iẓāfat syllable itself is flexible: long or short as the meter needs.

rules.title: iẓāfat after a written short vowel (dar-pa-e)

condition.ascii: a one-consonant word written with its short vowel (pa), then -e / -o-

rules.effect: the consonant keeps its short vowel; the iẓāfat is a separate flexible syllable: pa-e (- x)
rules.learner: In dar-pa-e the pa is already a syllable; the iẓāfat stands alone.

rules.title: o after a consonant
rules.effect: o joins the consonant as one flexible syllable: diin o dil = dii-no dil (= x =)

likelihood.handbook: the normal pattern

rules.learner: 'o' (and) after a consonant borrows it: diin-o-dil = dii-no-dil.

rules.title: Arabic C+C monosyllable + o: optional tashdīd

condition.word: two consonant letters with a short vowel between

rules.effect: ;xa-:to (- x) or ;xa:t-:to (= x)
rules.learner: Before 'o', a short Arabic word may double its last letter, less often than before an iẓāfat.

rules.title: o after alif
rules.effect: o is always an independent syllable (usually short); the aa before it is always long
rules.learner: After -aa, 'o' stands alone (usually short) and the -aa stays long: vafaa o (- = -).

rules.title: o after ii
rules.effect: usually an independent (short) o after a long ii; occasionally (Mir) ii becomes y: shaa-di-yo (= - x)
rules.learner: After -ii, 'o' usually stands alone: saa-da-gii o.

rules.title: o after e / o / uu / au / ai
rules.effect: usually the vowel becomes a consonant and joins o: mai o = ma-yo (- x), ;xusrau o = ;xus-ra-vo
rules.learner: After -e or -o, 'o' turns the vowel into y / v: mai o = ma-yo.

rules.title: o after h

condition.last_letter: h (gol he after a short vowel)

rules.effect: usually h + o one flexible syllable; sometimes h read as a vowel and o independent
rules.learner: After a final h, 'o' usually joins it (-ho); sometimes it stands alone.

rules.title: Weight of the o syllable
rules.effect: x; the independent o is usually short

likelihood.handbook: flexible; independent o usually short, at times long

rules.learner: The 'o' syllable is flexible; standing alone it is usually short.

rules.title: o after a written short vowel

condition.ascii: a one-consonant word written with its short vowel (pa), then -e / -o-

rules.effect: o is a separate flexible syllable
rules.learner: After a written short vowel, 'o' stands alone.

rules.title: al after a consonant
rules.effect: pretend the first word ends in an extra l: ((aalam ul-;Gaib = ((aa-la-mul ;Gai-b; after al scansion starts afresh
rules.learner: ul- sticks to the word before it as an extra -ul; the next word starts fresh.

rules.title: al after a vowel
rules.effect: the vowel shortens: bi al-kul = bil-kul, fii al-;haal = fil-;haal, ;zuu al-fiqaar = ;zul-fi-qaar

shorten.handbook: reality is invariably shorter than the appearance

rules.learner: Before al, a final vowel is swallowed: fii al-;haal is fil-;haal.

rules.title: Word-final ((ain after a long vowel
rules.effect: an extra short syllable, from orthography, though rarely heard: shuruu(( = shu-ruu-(( (- = -)
rules.learner: A final ع after a long vowel is a short syllable even if you don't hear it: shu-ruu-((.

rules.title: Long vowel + two consonants at word end

condition.word_final: long vowel + C + C (dost, raast, gosht, koft, kaard)

rules.effect: the two consonants act as one letter: dost = do-st (= -); VERY rarely (= - -) or (=); NEVER (= =)
rules.learner: dost, gosht, raast end in (= -): the last two consonants count as one short. Before an iẓāfat they split normally: do-s-te.

rules.title: Suppressed vao after ;x
rules.effect: the vao is not scanned: ;xvud = ;xud (=), ;xvaab = ;xaab (= -)

likelihood.handbook: MOST (;x+o+C), wherever (;x+o+a)

rules.learner: In ;xvaab and ;xvud the و is silent: ;xaab, ;xud.

rules.title: piyaalah as pyaalah
rules.effect: normally pi-yaa-lah (- = x); rarely pyaa-lah (= x)
rules.learner: piyaalah is normally pi-yaa-lah; rarely pyaa-lah.

rules.title: Indic initial conjuncts (pyaar, byaah, dhyaan)

condition.word_initial: consonant with no vowel + consonant (mostly y) + vowel

rules.effect: the two consonants act as one: pyaar = pyaa-r (= -)

separate.handbook: once in a while... quite rare

rules.learner: In pyaar, byaah, kyaa the first two consonants blend into one: pyaa-r (= -).

rules.title: tumhaaraa, tumhe;N, unho;N: h as aspirator
rules.effect: scanned as if the gol he were do-chashmii: tumhaaraa (- = x), tumhe;N (- x)
rules.learner: tumhaaraa is tu-mhaa-raa (- = x): the h behaves like the ھ of bh, not a letter.

rules.title: Perfect forms of honaa
rules.effect: scanned as pronounced hu))aa (- x), not as spelled
rules.implemented: engine (ASCII spelling huu))- is normalised; Urdu via the corpus lexicon)
rules.learner: ہوا is hu-))aa (- x), whatever the spelling suggests.

rules.title: tanvīn
rules.effect: read as -an: faura:n = fau-ran (= =)
rules.learner: فوراً ends in -an: fau-ran.

rules.title: Dagger alif
rules.effect: scanned as a normal alif (lail;aa = lai-laa)
rules.learner: The small standing alif counts as a full alif: lail;aa = lai-laa.

rules.title: Dagger alif + iẓāfat read as ii
rules.effect: usually as alif (lail;aa-e = lai-laa-e); sometimes as ii, which then becomes y: da((v;aa-e = da((-va-ye
rules.learner: دعویٰ with an iẓāfat can scan da((-va-ye, as if it ended in ii.

rules.title: Word-final hamza after alif
rules.effect: usually not scanned; if scanned, an extra short
rules.learner: umaraa)) — the final hamza is almost never counted.

rules.title: all;aah
rules.effect: (= = -) or, less commonly, (= =)
rules.learner: all;aah is al-l;aa-h (= = -), or less often (= =).

rules.title: khaṛī zer / do zer
rules.effect: read as -hii / -in
rules.implemented: not-implemented (very rare; no case in the corpora)
rules.learner: A standing zer under a final h reads -hii.

rules.title: Glossary scansions the general rules do not produce
rules.effect: offer the glossary's scansion as an alternative reading (pahu;Nchaa = p'hu;N-chaa (= x), tevrii = tev-rii (= x), dobaarah (x = x) ...)

alt.handbook: the glossary lists the special scansion

rules.learner: Some words have special scansions listed in the handbook's glossary; the engine offers them.

rules.title: pahu;Nch- scanned without its u
rules.effect: the transcription's u is not in the Urdu spelling (پہنچ); pahu;Nchaa = p'hu;N-chaa (= x)
rules.learner: pahu;Nchaa scans p'hu;N-chaa (= x): Urdu spells it پہنچا, with no vowel after the h.

rules.title: Every meter ends in a long syllable
rules.effect: the last scanned syllable is long (a cheat syllable may follow)
rules.learner: Every line ends on a long beat.

rules.title: Never three shorts in a row
rules.effect: a flexible syllable between two shorts must be long; three definite shorts are impossible
rules.learner: Three short syllables never come in a row. If they seem to, one of them must be long.

rules.title: Cheat syllable at line end

condition.syllable: word-final, one-letter short, or hamza + vowel

rules.effect: an extra unscanned short after the final long
rules.learner: A line may end with one extra short (a one-letter syllable like the -t of dost); it is not counted. Meter #26 does not allow it.

rules.title: Cheat syllable before the caesura
rules.effect: an extra unscanned short before the break
rules.learner: Meters with a mid-line break (#2, 4, 7, 20, 21, 22, 25, 36) also allow an extra short just before the break.

rules.title: Freely combinable meter pairs
rules.effect: two shorts may replace the next-to-last long (third syllable for #1/#9); lines of a pair mix freely
rules.learner: Some meters come in pairs that differ only by (- -) for (=) near the end; poets mix them freely.

rules.title: First syllable of #14–#19
rules.effect: the first syllable (normally long) may be short at will
rules.learner: In meters #14–#19 the first syllable can be long or short.

rules.title: Flexible form of #6
rules.effect: any odd-numbered long may be replaced by two shorts
rules.learner: Meter #6 has a rare flexible form where longs split into two shorts.

rules.title: taskīn-e ausaṭ: two shorts replaced by a long
rules.effect: middle (- -) as (=)

used.handbook: the only such example I have ever seen

rules.learner: Very rarely (one line of Mir in #8) two middle shorts are replaced by one long.

rules.title: Hindi meter: line length
rules.effect: 15 long-equivalents usual; 14 and 16 also used (two shorts = one long)
rules.learner: Mir's Hindi meter counts beats: usually 15 longs' worth, where two shorts make one long.

rules.title: Hindi meter: shorts in pairs
rules.effect: short syllables occur in pairs; a pair may be separated by at most one long (syncopation - = -); the last syllable is long; cheat allowed at the end but never at the break
rules.learner: In the Hindi meter shorts come in pairs (occasionally split by one long).

rules.title: Hindi meter: Russell's model
rules.effect: pairs normally replace even-numbered longs except the 8th; elsewhere is off-model

off-model.handbook: Mir uses it in more complex ways

rules.learner: A pair of shorts usually stands where an even-numbered long would be.

rules.title: Hindi meter: syncopated (- = -)
rules.effect: a pair of shorts split by one long
rules.learner: Now and then a long sits between the two shorts of a pair: - = -.

rules.title: rubāʿī meters
rules.effect: 12 forms: 10 long-equivalents; 3rd/6th/9th long may be two shorts; 6th pair may surround the 5th
rules.implemented: meter (as 12 fixed patterns, penalised outside quatrains)
rules.learner: The rubāʿī uses its own 12 related patterns.

rules.title: Scan several lines together
rules.effect: all lines share one meter; columns of flexibles resolve by the meter; a column of flexibles usually means short
rules.learner: One line can mislead; eight lines rarely do. Scan the whole ghazal and let the columns decide.

rules.title: Pritchett-ASCII is taken as written
rules.effect: short vowels, iẓāfat (-e), o (-o-), tashdīd (doubled letter), ;N vs n, ((ain and hamza are all explicit; no transcription hypotheses are generated
rules.learner: In the romanised text every vowel and iẓāfat is written, so only real prosodic choices remain.

rules.title: ASCII n after a long vowel may stand for ;N

condition.letter: n after a long vowel, before a consonant, inside a word

rules.effect: read as nasalisation (;Dhuun;Dhaa = ;Dhuu;N;Dhaa)

nasal.handbook: 7: the possibility of confusion between n and ;N

rules.learner: If a transcription writes n after a long vowel before another consonant, it may really be a nasal ;N.

rules.title: Known word: corpus readings
rules.effect: offer each attested Pritchett transcription, weighted by frequency
rules.learner: For a known word the engine uses the ways Pritchett actually transcribed it (e.g. کیا = kyaa or kiyaa).

rules.title: Unwritten short vowels

condition.consonant: not followed by a vowel letter

rules.effect: hypothesise a short vowel or none after each consonant; probabilities learned from the ASCII corpus by letter context

likelihood.handbook: orthography alone is often sufficient (4.1); otherwise follow pronunciation (1.4)

rules.learner: Urdu script rarely writes short vowels, so the engine has to guess where they are.

rules.title: و / ی: vowel or consonant
rules.effect: vowel (o/uu/au, ii/e/ai) or consonant (v, y); the amphibious role of o ii e (7)
rules.learner: و and ی can be vowels (o, ii) or consonants (v, y); the meter can tell you which.

rules.title: ن before a consonant: n or ;N
rules.effect: after a long vowel usually ;N (not a letter); after a short vowel usually n, except Indic first syllables (ha;Nsnaa, mu;Nh)

likelihood.handbook: in general ;N can occur only after long vowels

rules.learner: Medial ن after a long vowel is usually just nasalisation (aa;Nkh); after a short vowel it is usually a full n (rang).

rules.title: Unwritten iẓāfat
rules.effect: hypothesise an iẓāfat anyway

likelihood.handbook: the possible presence of an iẓāfat even if it is not written

rules.learner: Printed Urdu usually leaves out the iẓāfat zer; the meter tells you where it must be.

rules.title: Written iẓāfat forms

marks: ئے / ۓ after alif or vao

rules.effect: iẓāfat present (ئے after a vowel can also be a verb ending: jaa))e)
rules.learner: ۂ, a final zer, or ئے after -aa all mark an iẓāfat.

rules.title: Unwritten tashdīd
rules.effect: hypothesise a doubled letter

likelihood.handbook: often the tashdiid is not written, but must nevertheless be assumed

rules.learner: A tashdīd is often left unwritten (مدت = mud-dat); if a syllable is missing, look for one.

rules.title: ek / ik miswritten
rules.effect: the calligrapher may have written ek for ik or the reverse

swapped.handbook: the most common possibility of this kind

rules.learner: If a line is one short too many, check whether ایک should be اک.

rules.title: Scribal slips: kar/ke, shaah/shah
rules.effect: a copying error, much more likely than a poet writing out of meter

slip.handbook: editors and calligraphers do often make mistakes

rules.learner: When nothing else explains a limp, suspect the text: kar for ke, shaah for shah.

rules.title: gol he written for do-chashmī (older texts) and vice versa

condition.letter: ہ after an aspirable consonant, or decorative ھ

rules.effect: treat by function: aspiration is invisible, gol he is a letter
rules.learner: Older books write ہ for ھ; what matters is whether it is an aspiration or a real h.
